## Discussion

To sum up, this study presents the results of a prospective, parallel‑group, placebo‑controlled randomized clinical trial evaluating a WBI for individuals who committed sexual offenses against children. Contrary to our primary hypothesis, the intervention did not result in a significant reduction of psychologically meaningful risk factors as assessed by the primary outcome (CARES). This finding is in line with recent literature showing that studies with high methodological quality tend to report smaller or null effects. Importantly, the low rate of reoffenses during participation and the low frequency of adverse events indicate that the intervention can be delivered without evident harm to participants or society. Dropout rates were high but comparable to those observed in the Prevent It intervention. At present, outcome assessment relies exclusively on self‑reports, and no scale assessing impression management was applied. Furthermore, the achieved sample size was smaller than the predefined target, rendering the study underpowered. Official recidivism data will only become available at the end of 2030, which will be necessary to draw definitive conclusions regarding long‑term effectiveness.

In this worldwide first randomized placebo‑controlled clinical trial of a WBI for tertiary prevention in individuals who committed sexual offenses against children, no significant reduction of risk factors in the intervention arm compared with the placebo arm was observed on the primary endpoint. Among secondary outcomes, several risk factors showed significant within‑group pre–post changes in the intervention arm in line with our hypotheses, most notably increased treatment readiness (CVTRQ), reduced sexual interest in children (ESIQ), and increased impulsivity‑related difficulties (DERS impulsivity subscale). The placebo arm showed an isolated improvement in perceived social support (F‑Soz‑U). Between‑group difference scores confirmed a significant reduction in self‑reported sexual interest in children in the intervention group, whereas all other outcomes yielded non‑significant or non‑robust results. Ancillary analyses demonstrated statistically robust improvements in working alliance ratings (WAI‑SR) with both online coaches and community supervisors in the intervention group, while no comparable changes occurred in the placebo arm. Importantly, no evidence emerged for an increased risk of recidivism or clinically relevant deterioration in mental well‑being attributable to the intervention. However, none of the statistically significant self‑reported effects reached clinical significance as defined by the Reliable Change Index [Jacobson and Truax (1991)], rendering the overall effectiveness of the WBI questionable.
The present trial stands in contrast to the only other placebo‑controlled WBI study in this population, Prevent It (Lätth et al., 2022), which reported a small but significant effect in favor of the intervention. Conceptually, the WBI evaluated here differs substantially from Prevent It, as it is more complex, more intensive, and exclusively targets psychologically meaningful risk factors derived from prior empirical and theoretical work. Meta‑meta‑analytic evidence suggests that higher treatment intensity is generally associated with larger effects [@olverSexualOffenseTreatment2025], yet this relationship did not translate into superior outcomes in the present online format. Although the dropout rate was high, it was not higher than in Prevent It. These findings suggest that increased complexity and intensity alone do not guarantee improved effectiveness in web‑based interventions.

A key novel finding of this study is the very low number of adverse events and reoffenses during participation, which appears comparable to previous findings reported by Lätth et al. (2022) and potentially other treatment programs such as SOTP. This supports the conclusion that the WBI does not increase risk. At the same time, the observed increase in impulsivity highlights the necessity of rigorous evaluation prior to implementation, particularly in forensic contexts. Numerous online interventions are already publicly available and widely promoted despite lacking empirical evaluation, raising the possibility that some may cause more harm than benefit.
For the first time, using a methodologically rigorous placebo‑controlled design, this study demonstrates no reduction in self‑reported risk factors through a WBI compared with an online placebo condition. This contrasts with the only previous placebo‑controlled study, which reported a small effect favoring the intervention arm based on self‑report measures. Notably, self‑report instruments have since been further evaluated, including a recent validation of the CHiXX+ [NEUE STUDIE mit Lätth, die das CHiXX+ validiert hat]. In contrast, face‑to‑face programs have previously demonstrated self‑reported effects (Wild et al.), even in smaller samples without control groups, using the same questionnaires for which no effects were observed in the present study. These findings underscore that digitalization of an effective face‑to‑face treatment does not automatically preserve its effectiveness, even when core therapeutic content remains unchanged.
The finding that impulsivity decreased in the placebo arm in Module 3 further illustrates the importance of evaluating interventions prior to implementation in forensic settings. Without proper evaluation, it remains unclear whether certain intervention components may have unintended negative effects. This is particularly relevant given the increasing availability of unevaluated online interventions.

A central controversy addressed by this study concerns the modifiability of sexual interest in children. While the prevailing clinical view assumes limited changeability, this remains an active scientific debate. McPhail et al. (2020) reported indications of treatment‑related changes in sexual interest in the most recent meta‑analysis, although none of the included studies employed an adequate control group. Against this background, the present placebo‑controlled trial provides the first experimental evidence for a statistically significant reduction in sexual interest in children. However, the magnitude of change was small and did not reach clinical significance, warranting cautious interpretation.

The representativeness of the study population is limited by a potential volunteer effect. At the same time, to our knowledge, this is the first randomized clinical trial in Germany recruiting participants from almost all federal states. Financial compensation was provided to reduce potential volunteer bias. Nevertheless, unrestricted access to all eligible probation clients was not possible, and selective referral by probation officers cannot be ruled out.

Several mechanisms may underlie the null findings on the primary outcome. Dropout may have been driven in part by participants’ interest in receiving official documentation for court rather than financial compensation resulting in low protocol adherence and motivation. Moreover, baseline levels of several secondary outcomes risk factors were low, suggesting a violation of the need principle of the RNR model. With the exception of Module five, which allowed individual selection of offense‑supportive cognitions, intervention content was not individualized based on baseline risk levels. Meta‑analyses indicate that programs targeting high‑risk individuals and relevant needs yield larger effects, yet the present study reflects real‑world practice, where many low‑risk individuals receive mandatory treatment despite limited need. This approach may be financially and logistically motivated in times of staff shortages but illustrates the current state of care.

Participants in the intervention arm consistently required more time to complete modules than recommended and more time than participants in the placebo arm. Both MMRM and descriptive analyses indicated a steadily increasing total completion time, with growing divergence between groups, although pairwise differences were attenuated after correction for multiple testing. This prolonged duration may have compromised comparability at later assessments and contributed to dropout.

The study was underpowered to detect small effects, as the predefined sample size of 214 participants per arm required to detect effect sizes as small as d = 0.2 was not reached. Furthermore, it was not possible to recruit a fully representative sample of all individuals on probation due to restricted access and data protection regulations. Lack of direct contact with participants during the intervention further limited retention efforts, as reminders could only be communicated via supervisors. Many participants failed to complete the modules within the planned timeframe, which likely contributed to premature study termination. Despite being the largest sample to date in this research area, the study must therefore be considered undersampled, and small effects may have gone undetected. Accordingly, the findings should be interpreted with caution.
Another explanation for the absence of effects may be the predominance of low‑risk individuals in the sample. Whether low‑risk sexual offenders should be treated remains controversial [SOTP literature], although recent findings from secondary prevention indicate no increased risk associated with treatment [@franqueIndividualsVoluntaryTreatment2023]. 

Norm‑referenced secondary outcomes suggested that many participants scored within normal ranges, indicating limited severity of risk factors. Baseline characteristics further showed that most participants with court‑ordered treatment were not receiving face‑to‑face psychotherapy, highlighting a substantial care gap in Germany. At the same time, low baseline recidivism risk raises questions about the necessity of mandatory treatment from an RNR perspective, a practice that appears common in both Germany and Canada [@frankeEfficacyOutpatientTreatment2021; @mcpheePracticeSurveyCanadian2025].

Psychiatric burden in the sample was low, as indicated by PHQ‑D and WHO‑5 scores, which contrasts with previous literature reporting substantial psychological distress among individuals with sexual interest in children [Jahnke et al.; Beier review]. The low prevalence of self‑reported pedophilic disorder must be interpreted cautiously, as diagnoses were based on self‑report rather than clinical assessment.

The reliance on self‑report for the primary outcome represents another limitation. While self‑reports are controversial in this field, recent evidence suggests that self‑reported data collected in WBIs may still be informative regarding recidivism risk [recent Lätth study]. Nevertheless, impression management was not assessed, limiting the ability to account for response bias. Although officially recorded reoffenses are considered the gold standard outcome measure, they are insensitive, delayed, and provide little insight into treatment processes. Consequently, several authors have emphasized the importance of assessing within‑treatment changes in risk factors [@mannAssessingRiskSexual2010; @olverEvaluatingChangeMen2020]. The CARES is a relatively new instrument, and data linking it to official recidivism outcomes are not yet available.

Finally, it is possible that the placebo condition produced effects that obscured between‑group differences. Health‑related topics such as sleep, exercise, and nutrition may improve overall life satisfaction, aligning with the Good Lives Model [LIT]. However, no effects were observed on WHO‑5 well‑being, the closest proxy for Good Lives outcomes assessed in this study.

Future research should include face‑to‑face and waiting‑list control groups to clarify the relative effectiveness of WBIs, revise Module 3, apply stricter RNR‑based individualization, and test blended approaches combining digital content with regular personal contact to improve adherence. The intervention is currently only available in German, limiting its international applicability.

From a clinical and policy perspective, the findings caution against recommending existing online interventions without rigorous evaluation, as effectiveness cannot be inferred from face‑to‑face evidence. While secondary outcomes indicate a reduction in sexual interest in children—a key risk factor for recidivism—impulsivity increased in the intervention arm, underscoring the importance of careful evaluation. Only interventions with high methodological quality should be implemented. Although mandatory treatment for low‑risk individuals appears questionable, selected modules of the WBI may already be useful in practice, particularly for strengthening therapeutic alliance with community supervisors or online coaches.
